Baby & Child

Supporting your teenager through romantic relationships

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When a teenager says they are in love, a parent may feel protective, uncertain or unprepared. Taking their feelings seriously does not mean stepping back from safety. You can stay involved, explain reasonable expectations and help them recognise respect, pressure and control. The aim is to remain a dependable adult while your teenager learns to make relationship decisions.

Romantic feelings deserve respect, without pressure to date

A crush or a relationship can feel important even when it is new or does not last. Teenagers may learn about communication, preferences and emotional closeness through these experiences. Others have little interest in dating, and that is normal too. Do not treat having a partner as a milestone they must reach or assume who they will be attracted to.

Neither romance nor being single is automatically good or bad for wellbeing. What matters includes how people treat one another, whether choices are free and whether the relationship leaves room for the rest of life. Avoid predicting poor grades, depression or a ruined future simply because your teenager has romantic feelings. Notice actual difficulties and ask what is happening.

Begin with curiosity rather than ridicule or interrogation

Choose an ordinary, private moment and ask what they enjoy about the person or how spending time together feels. Let them finish before giving advice. A comment such as “This sounds important to you” can acknowledge the feeling without approving every plan. Avoid jokes about their crush, public teasing or comparisons with siblings and your own teenage experiences.

If they do not want to talk, leave the invitation open and return gently another time. Several brief conversations may be easier than one formal discussion. You can admit that the subject feels unfamiliar and still listen respectfully. Do not demand intimate details, impersonate a friend or set traps to catch them out; these approaches make an honest conversation harder.

Stay a parent who can listen and set limits

Warmth does not require becoming your teenager’s best friend or surrendering your adult responsibilities. Explain concerns in terms they can evaluate: an unsafe journey home, a large power imbalance or a plan that leaves no way to contact help. Ask for their view and distinguish a genuine safety concern from discomfort with a different personality, appearance or background.

Parents can also seek support for their own worries. A counsellor or another trusted adult can help you respond thoughtfully without making your teenager responsible for calming you. Avoid threats, hitting, humiliation or making affection conditional on ending a relationship. No parenting technique guarantees that a teenager will agree with you or that every relationship will go well.

Agree practical arrangements for seeing a partner

Discuss where they are going, who will be there, transport, a realistic return time and how to contact you if plans change. Get to know the person they are seeing when appropriate. Expectations should fit your teenager’s age, understanding, needs and the actual situation, and should be revisited as circumstances change. Explain the reason for a limit rather than relying only on “because I said so”.

Keep a route home available if a meeting becomes uncomfortable. For example, agree how they can ask you or another trusted adult for a lift. Deal with immediate safety first; a later conversation can address a broken household rule. Privacy matters, but it does not require ignoring a concrete threat. If protection requires more direct action, explain the concern as safely as possible and obtain appropriate advice.

Make respect and consent concrete

Ask whether both people can disagree, say no and spend time with friends without fear of punishment. Healthy relationships allow separate interests and do not require constant availability. A disagreement can be ordinary; intimidation, threats and forced compliance are different. Encourage your teenager to show the same respect for another person’s choices that they expect for their own.

Consent involves a freely made choice and can be withdrawn. A previous yes, gifts, a relationship label or fear of upsetting someone does not create an obligation to accept affection or sexual activity. No one should be pressured to prove love. Keep discussions about sexual health factual and age-appropriate, and help them access qualified advice. Local laws and confidentiality rules vary; a household rule is not a substitute for professional guidance.

Recognise when attention becomes control

Repeated demands for passwords, location updates or instant replies can be controlling rather than caring. Other concerns include isolating someone from friends, deciding what they wear, humiliating them or making them afraid to end a conversation. Harm can occur in person or through messages, and it is not limited to one gender or type of couple.

A mood change, private conversation or missed assignment does not by itself prove abuse. Look at the pattern and ask calmly about what you have noticed. Take a disclosure or a specific threat seriously even if there is no visible injury. If your teenager is the person using threats or control, respond promptly, stop the harmful behaviour and seek professional help rather than excusing it as passion.

Help the relationship fit alongside everyday life

Talk about preserving friendships, sleep, school commitments and activities your teenager values. This is not a demand to keep feelings small. It is a way to avoid making one relationship the only source of belonging or confidence. Ask which routines are becoming difficult and work on a manageable adjustment, such as protecting an evening for an existing activity.

If grades or participation change, explore the reasons instead of assuming romance is the cause. Stress, bullying, health problems and learning difficulties can also matter. Support from school or a healthcare professional may help when difficulties persist. Avoid turning every check-in into a performance review; your teenager should still be able to enjoy a relationship and talk about it.

Support a breakup without taking it over

A breakup or an unreturned crush may bring sadness, anger, embarrassment or relief. Listen without dismissing it as “only teenage love” or setting a deadline for feeling better. Offer company and ordinary activities, while allowing some space. You can acknowledge their hurt without insulting the other person or trying to arrange a reunion.

Respect a teenager’s choice to end a relationship, even if you liked the partner. Do not pressure them to stay to avoid hurting someone’s feelings. Encourage respectful endings when safe, but never require a private meeting with someone who is threatening or abusive. If unwanted contact or fear continues, seek specialist help with safety rather than treating it as ordinary heartbreak.

Respond to coercion or harm with support

If your teenager reports pressure, threats or violence, thank them for telling you and check whether they are safe now. Let them speak at their own pace and avoid blame. They do not need to prove that they resisted or made every decision perfectly to deserve help. Do not turn the situation into a family interrogation or a confrontation with the other person.

Contact an appropriate local safeguarding professional, healthcare service or specialist relationship-abuse service for advice about protection and next steps. Involve your teenager as far as it is safe and appropriate. Concern about an adult exploiting a young person or a marked power imbalance needs prompt attention. Do not ask a teenager to manage another person’s threats of self-harm by remaining in the relationship; obtain urgent professional help for the threat.

Know when additional help is needed

Seek help from a healthcare professional or counsellor when distress persists, disrupts everyday functioning or is worsening. Changes in sleep, loss of interest, withdrawal or difficulty attending school deserve attention without assuming a particular diagnosis. A young person with an existing mental health condition may need extra support after relationship difficulties. Another trusted adult may be easier to approach initially, and that can still be a useful route to care.

Talk of harming oneself or someone else, self-injury or unsafe behaviour needs immediate professional help. If there is immediate danger, serious injury or you cannot keep someone safe, contact local emergency services. Stay nearby when safe while help is arranged. Ordinary relationship conversations and a scheduled counselling appointment do not replace an urgent response.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Use specific relationship examples to discuss respect, consent and pressure, while keeping help available.

Agree practical boundaries appropriate to age, needs and risk; protect privacy without ignoring concrete safeguarding concerns.

Separate ordinary disappointment from persistent distress or danger, and arrange the level of support the situation requires.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to prepare a conversation and questions for a professional. BeMama cannot judge whether a relationship is safe, investigate abuse, establish legal consent or provide an emergency response.

When to seek help

Coercion, exploitation or violence needs prompt safeguarding support. Self-injury or talk of harming oneself or others needs immediate professional help; immediate danger, serious injury or inability to keep someone safe requires local emergency services. Do not require a teenager to remain in a relationship or meet a threatening person alone.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Take romantic feelings seriously while respecting a teenager’s choice not to date.
  • Use clear, proportionate arrangements for plans, contact and getting home.
  • Discuss consent, independence and the difference between care and control.
  • Offer support through rejection or a breakup without forcing a reunion or unsafe contact.
  • Respond promptly to coercion, persistent distress and immediate safety concerns.

Frequently asked questions

Why pay attention to a teenager’s romantic relationship?

It may be an important part of their emotional life. Support helps them think about respect, consent and practical safety. A relationship does not automatically cause academic or mental health problems; look at how it is affecting this particular young person.

How should I respond when my teenager says they are in love?

Listen without mocking or dismissing the feeling. Ask what they value about the relationship, explain specific safety concerns and agree practical expectations. You can remain a caring parent without trying to control every feeling or decision.

What if the relationship is taking over school and other activities?

Discuss what has changed and which commitments or friendships they want to protect. Work on a realistic balance and investigate other possible difficulties. Persistent problems or significant distress may need school or professional support.

What if I do not know how to handle it?

You can ask a qualified counsellor or another appropriate professional for help. Admit what you do not know, keep conversations respectful and avoid making the teenager responsible for your anxiety. Support is available before a situation becomes a crisis.

Should I take their phone to stop a relationship?

Automatic punishment or secret surveillance can make disclosure harder. Explain supervision and respond to the actual risk. A concrete threat may require immediate protective action and specialist advice; keeping the child safe takes priority over a dispute about household rules.

Is jealousy proof that someone cares?

Feeling jealous does not justify controlling another person. Demands for passwords, isolation, humiliation, threats or pressure are warning signs. A teenager should not have to give up friendships or freedom to refuse in order to keep a partner calm.

How can I help after a breakup?

Acknowledge the hurt, offer company and let recovery take its own course. Respect the choice to leave and avoid forcing reconciliation. Seek help for persistent or worsening distress, and get specialist advice if the former partner is threatening or will not stop unwanted contact.

When should I act urgently?

Seek prompt safeguarding advice for coercion, exploitation or violence. Self-injury or talk of harming anyone needs immediate professional help. Immediate danger, serious injury or inability to keep someone safe requires local emergency services; do not wait for a routine appointment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
